sections.h2: Where is the Franklin County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
The Franklin County Register of Deeds is at 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard in Louisburg, NC 27549, after a move made while the county courthouse is under construction. The mailing address is P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549, the phone is 919-496-3500 and the fax is 919-496-1457.

The county describes the office as the custodian of real estate documents for Franklin County that reach back to 1776. For a sale anywhere in Franklin County, this is the office that holds the deed you received, the deed of trust on it and any plat or power of attorney tied to the parcel. Credit card payments are available. Because the office relocated recently, check the county page before you drive over with a document, and mail or e-record when you can.

sections.h2: What records does the Franklin County office keep?
sections.html:
Land records and vital records share one counter, and the land side matters most to a seller. For a home sale the land records matter most.

  • Deeds and deeds of trust, the documents that move title and secure a loan.
  • Powers of attorney, assumed names, maps and other papers connected to real property.
  • Military discharge records.
  • Birth and death certificates back to 1913 for events in Franklin County, and marriage certificates back to 1869, with a bond book that carries marriage information from 1779.

The office can also print birth and death certificates from the state system for North Carolina events, and it takes online orders for certified or regular copies of vital records through a county vendor. A seller dealing with an inherited house often needs a death certificate and the old deed from the same visit.

sections.h2: Does Franklin County require tax certification before a deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Yes. A deed moving real property is turned away unless the Tax Collector first certifies that no delinquent ad valorem or other administered tax is a lien on it. The county has applied this rule since April 1, 2015.

The Collections Department stamps deeds free of charge on weekdays between 8 am and 5 pm, excluding county holidays. Walk the deed in before recording, or mail it to the Franklin County Tax Collector, P.O. Box 503, Louisburg, NC 27549, Attention: Tax Certification. The eRecording system forwards deeds to the tax office on its own. Electronic recordings that need the stamp must reach the tax department by 4:30 pm, so a closing that wraps up late should send its package early.

For a seller with back taxes, this is where the problem surfaces. The deed waits until the balance is cleared or the closing agent pays it out of the proceeds.

sections.h2: Can I record a Franklin County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. Title companies, banks, attorneys and private individuals can all submit electronically, and every document type is accepted except UCC filings.

The county names three authorized providers: CSC eRecording Solutions (866-652-0111), Simplifile (800-460-5657) and the ePN eRecording Partners Network (888-325-3365). Its stated benefits are quicker recording, lower postage and courier spending, fewer rejected documents and added security. Closing attorneys normally choose the provider, so a seller rarely sets this up personally. Ask which day your closing will be recorded.

sections.h2: What will a Franklin County closing pay at the Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
Two charges apply at the counter: a page-based recording fee and a tax tied to the sale price.

For the recording fee, the state tier is $26 for a general instrument through page 15, with $4 added for every page after that. A deed of trust is $64 through page 35. Recording the release of a paid-off loan is free. A certified copy starts at $5, and a document that does not meet the standard format costs $25 more.

The deed tax is $1 for every $500 of price or value, counting any leftover fraction as a full $500. The party giving up the property pays it at the register of deeds window ahead of recording, and the proceeds are divided between the county and state revenue. Your settlement statement will carry the final number.

sections.h2: How do Franklin County tax bills affect a seller?
sections.html:
Franklin County real estate tax is due September 1 for the current tax year, and bills for 2026 become delinquent on January 6, 2027. The county mails bills in late July to early August, and money received before September 1 can earn a discount.

When a house sells after the bill arrives, the county tells the former owner to hand the bill to the buyer unless the former owner will pay it. Agreements between buyers, sellers and attorneys are not the tax office's concern, and because tax is a lien on real estate, the buyer wants everything settled at closing. A mortgage company that escrows tax still causes the bill to be mailed to the owner, and the county suggests checking in the second week of September that the lender paid. The county also bills a Solid Waste Availability Fee for each electrical connection, set each year in the budget ordinance, and it does not depend on full-time residence.

sections.h2: What is the process to dispute a Franklin County assessed value?
sections.html:
An owner files the Board of Equalization and Review form between January 1 and the board's adjournment, which usually falls in May. A change-of-value notice opens a separate 30-day window.

Staff look at the file first. Anything they cannot settle goes to the board, which mails its decision. The current revaluation took effect January 1, 2024, so the county wants evidence tied to that date. Higher bills, fixed income and market drops after January 1, 2024 are not legal grounds. Comparable properties with lower values, comparable sales before that date, unrepaired fire or storm damage, a denied septic permit and documented cleanup costs are. The owner carries the burden of proof. If the worry is affordability, ask the tax office about relief programs.

sections.h2: Why does recording order matter on a Franklin County sale?
sections.html:
Registration time decides priority. Under G.S. 47-18, a deed, option, lease longer than three years and similar interests do not bind lien creditors or paying buyers until they are registered in the county where the land sits.

That explains why closings are timed around recording cutoffs, and why an unrecorded deed from a former owner can stall a new sale. If an inherited Franklin County house still shows the deceased relative as owner, check the index before you list and ask your closing attorney what must be recorded first.

faqs.q: Is the Franklin County Register of Deeds in the courthouse?
faqs.a: No, not at present. The office now sits at 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard in Louisburg while the courthouse is under construction. Mail goes to P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549, and the phone is 919-496-3500.

faqs.q: Do I need a tax certification stamp to record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes, for any deed that transfers real property. The Tax Collector must certify there is no delinquent tax lien, free of charge on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. eRecording sends the deed to the tax office for you.

faqs.q: What does Franklin County charge to record?
faqs.a: The statewide tier applies: $26 through page 15 for a general instrument and $64 through page 35 for a deed of trust, plus $4 per extra page. Confirm with the office before mailing a long document.

faqs.q: Can a title company record electronically in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The office accepts all document types electronically except UCC filings, through CSC, Simplifile or the ePN network. The company or closing attorney normally handles the submission.

faqs.q: Who pays the North Carolina deed excise tax?
faqs.a: The seller, as transferor, settles it with the register of deeds ahead of recording. The rate is one dollar per $500 of value. The settlement statement shows the amount.
